body_markdown:
Many of us here at Hagerty are unabashed[AMC fans](https://www.hagerty.com/media/lists/celebrate-70-years-of-amc-with-10-of-our-favorite-models/) . We just love an underdog. Still, when we spotted this AMC Spirit at SEMA, we were shocked that the unassuming hatchback could look so right. Despite their clean ’80s lines, Spirits have never been terribly popular among enthusiasts. We had to learn more about this clean build, so we spoke to its owner, Miranda Rumfelt.


Rumfelt works at General Motors, sculpting clay for concept cars. One piece she’s worked on that you’ve probably seen is the all-electric[Corvette CX concept](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/the-first-corvette-concepts-since-2009-seek-to-elevate-the-marque/) . We wondered how her AMC project car would go over with her coworkers, but she reminded us that it’s powered by a Chevy 383 stroker, and there are plenty of AC Delco parts used in the build. Fair enough.


The interior, which normally would have featured woodgrain trim, was finished in black and gunmetal. It’s accented by a Grant steering wheel, a Lokar shifter, and a new set of bucket seats.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


“My dad actually collects AMCs,” Rumfelt said. “He has quite a few of them. He has an AMX, he has a Javelin, he has a Gremlin…” About 10 years ago, when Rumfelt was in high school, she wanted a car she could work on with her dad. Since he already had a Gremlin, why not the car that replaced the Gremlin in AMC’s lineup? This Spirit already had a Chevy 383 swapped in, but it was modified for drag racing and was in pretty rough shape. Still, she saw the potential. Rumfelt drove the car for more than seven years before she decided it was due for a full transformation. With her background in design and a side business as a rendering artist for project cars, it didn’t take her long to come up with a plan for her dream Spirit.


The 383 Chevy is bolted to a Gearstar 4L60E transmission that uses a US Shift standalone transmission controller. Output is somewhere in the neighborhood of 500 horsepower.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


The 1979 Spirit was the last AMC car to use a V-8. “In ’83, you couldn’t get a Spirit AMX,” Rumfelt explained. “Technically, this actual vehicle is a Spirit GT.” In 1983, this car would have had a set of turbine wheels and an AMC inline-six, still quite a lot of engine for such a small car. Now it’s running with a lot more power. The 383 Chevy small-block uses a Holley Hi-Ram Front Feed intake manifold, and it runs on Holley’s Terminator EFI. “Almost every single thing on this car is out of a Summit Racing catalog,” Rumfelt said, with one exception. Although Chevy small-blocks have been bolted into just about everything, it was impossible to find a set of headers to fit one in an AMC compact. Rumfelt’s partner on the build, Brandon Tregembo, fabricated those from stainless steel with the appropriate flange and an assortment of U-bends.


“My favorite thing about the overall build is really just the whole theme of having this nice black cherry color with all of the black accents,” said Rumfelt. There are a few pieces of trim that were painted gun metal, and even fewer that were left in stainless steel. Most of it would have been chrome. “All of that got blacked out,” Rumfelt explained. “The AMX badge would have been a bulky thing in the middle,” she said as she gestured to the grille. “I’ve got just a little guy down there in the corner, just kind of an accent.”


The 4×6-inch LED lights are from Dapper Lighting.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


“Every single thing on this car, we did, and nothing was sent out,” Rumfelt explained. She and Tregembo completely reworked the car in two and a half years inside her garage. Tregembo fabricated the front splitter and she used a rotisserie to get the underside of the body smoothed and prepped for paint. As you might expect, a 40-year-old car from the Midwest needed some rust repair, and they handled that as well. “The garage that we did it in is actually attached to my house, so I tell people, quite literally, everything was done in-house,” said Rumfelt.


Nitto tires are mounted to Konig Ampliform wheels. A Wilwood brake kit increases stopping power.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


New taillights were molded from the originals using clear acrylic.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


In addition to all of the rust repair and fixing all of the seemingly unnecessary holes cut in the body by the previous owner, Rumfelt shaved the rear marker lights and made sleek new marker lights up front. The paint is a custom mix from Glasurit. “I’ve painted other cars before,” she said, “but never one of my own, which was a little bit more intimidating.”


Rumfelt and Tregembo have a series of videos chronicling the Spirit’s build;[you can see the first part here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qTpsYIbqld0) . If you’d like to see it in person, she has plans to bring it to the Detroit Autorama and perhaps drive it on Hot Rod Power Tour.
